---
title: "Mixture of Experts (MoE)"
description: "A model architecture that routes each input to a subset of specialized expert networks."
term: "Mixture of Experts (MoE)"
letter: "M"
category: "LLM Engineering"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

A Mixture of Experts model contains multiple expert networks and a router that
chooses which experts process each input. A sparse MoE activates only a small
number of experts for a token, allowing a model to have many parameters
without running every parameter for every token.

## Technical explanation

An MoE layer commonly computes routing scores for each token, selects one or
more experts, and combines their outputs using routing weights. If $E_j$ is
expert $j$ and $g_j(x)$ is its gate weight, a dense combination would be
$\sum_j g_j(x)E_j(x)$. Sparse MoE restricts this sum to selected experts.

Routing capacity, token dropping or rerouting, and auxiliary balancing losses
are important implementation details. Uneven routing can overload some
experts while leaving others underused.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

MoE architectures can increase model capacity while limiting per-token
computation compared with a similarly sized dense model. Their routing and
expert placement introduce systems challenges such as load balancing,
communication overhead, and memory use.

## How it works

1. A router scores experts for an input token.
2. The system selects the top expert or experts.
3. The selected expert networks transform the token representation.
4. The router combines the outputs and passes the result onward.

The highlighted experts are active in this simplified example; real routing
decisions and expert counts depend on the architecture.

## Practical example

An MoE language model may route different tokens to different expert
feed-forward networks. For each token, only selected experts run, while the
router and shared parts of the model remain involved.

## Common misconceptions

- MoE does not mean each expert is automatically a human-interpretable specialist.
- A larger total parameter count does not mean every parameter is used for every token.
- Sparse computation can be offset by routing, communication, and memory costs.
